findings.title: [P1] Keep the branch argument out of the shell
findings.body: When `branch` contains shell syntax such as `HEAD; <command>`, `exec` interprets it and runs the appended command with the application's privileges. The previous `execFile("git", ["show", branch])` passed the value as a literal argument. Retain argv-based execution to prevent command injection and shell-created child-process lifecycle issues.

findings.title: [P2] Keep the returned child tied to Git so cancellation remains effective
findings.body:
`exec()` returns the shell process rather than the Git process. On POSIX, shell syntax in `branch`—including valid ref characters such as `&`—can launch Git or another command as a child/background process. The shell may emit `exit` before that work finishes, and calling `.kill()` on the returned child can leave descendants running, breaking completion and cancellation semantics.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Keep the branch argument out of the shell
findings.body:
`exec` interpolates `branch` into a shell command. On POSIX, input such as `HEAD; <arbitrary-command>` executes that command with the process’s privileges. Semicolons and other shell metacharacters are also valid in Git ref names, so even legitimate branches can trigger parsing. Preserve `execFile("git", ["show", branch])`.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Pass the branch as an `execFile` argument instead of interpolating it into a shell command
findings.body:
`exec` invokes a shell, so an attacker-controlled branch such as `main; rm -rf /tmp/data` executes arbitrary commands with the application’s privileges. The previous `execFile` implementation treated the branch solely as a Git argument.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Preserve argv-based execution to prevent unbounded subprocesses
findings.body:
On POSIX, `branch` is shell-expanded. A valid Git branch name such as `$(yes)` causes command substitution before Git starts; `yes` runs indefinitely while the shell waits and accumulates output, consuming CPU/memory and hanging the operation. The previous `execFile` call treated this name literally.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._
